content: The Second WHO Consultation on the Translation of Tuberculosis (TB) Research into Global Policy Guidelines, held on March 15–16, 2022, focused on advancing evidence-based policies for TB prevention, diagnosis, treatment, and care. The meeting brought together scientists, public health experts, civil society representatives, and country stakeholders to address emerging needs in global TB policy and align efforts with the WHO End TB Strategy. Abbreviations and Acronyms Key terms used in the report include: DST: Drug Susceptibility Testing DS-TB: Drug-Susceptible Tuberculosis DR-TB: Drug-Resistant Tuberculosis GTB: Global Tuberculosis Programme IPC: Infection Prevention and Control TPT: TB Preventive Therapy WHO: World Health Organization Background The WHO Global Tuberculosis Programme (GTB) is tasked with developing and disseminating evidence-based policies for TB prevention, diagnosis, treatment, and care. Regular evidence reviews and assessments of country needs are integral to this mandate. The consultation aimed to: 1. Present progress and plans for reviewing WHO TB policy guidance for 2022–2023. 2. Exchange views on emerging policy needs based on current evidence. Screening and Prevention Dennis Falzon presented WHO’s latest consolidated guidance on TB preventive treatment (TPT), infection prevention and control (IPC), and TB screening. Updates to the IPC handbook and guidelines were shared, along with developments in biomarkers and digital adherence technologies. Key discussion points included: 1. Awareness of ongoing research that could influence current recommendations on TB screening, TPT, and IPC. 2. Agreement on proposed strategies and identification of additional country needs. Diagnostics Nazir Ismail discussed updates on TB diagnostics, including the use of alternative interferon-gamma release assays for TB infection diagnosis and WHO’s first catalog of Mycobacterium tuberculosis genome mutations. The shift to class-based recommendations for diagnostics was highlighted to enhance market competition and provide countries with more options. Emerging areas of focus include subclinical TB and host-based diagnostics. Key discussion points included: 1. Identification of critical evidence gaps and upcoming studies. 2. Enhancing implementation of global TB policy guidance. 3. Exploring new research initiatives. Treatment Fuad Mirzayev reviewed the evolution of WHO TB treatment guidelines over the past 25 years. Recent updates for drug-susceptible TB (DS-TB) and drug-resistant TB (DR-TB) treatment were presented, along with ongoing clinical and operational research projects. Key discussion points included: 1. Addressing evidence gaps and promoting research in critical areas. 2. Identifying emerging needs in TB treatment policies and operational guidance. 3. Supporting programs with standardized decision-making for shorter DS-TB treatment options. Key Recommendations and Research Priorities 1. Screening and Prevention: Support rapid scale-up of new interventions for drug-resistant TB contacts if ongoing trials (e.g., VQUIN and TB-CHAMP) yield positive results. Update TB policy recommendations for co-administration of antiretroviral therapy and short-course TPT for people with HIV. Prioritize updates on short-course TPT regimens for young children, including 3HP (weekly rifapentine plus isoniazid for three months) and 1HP (daily rifapentine plus isoniazid for one month). 2. Diagnostics: Develop non-sputum-based TB detection tests, particularly for children. Improve sensitivity and specificity of existing biomarker tests, such as LF-LAM. Explore integrated diagnostic platforms for TB and other airborne pathogens. 3. Treatment: Define the role of the new six-month all-oral regimen versus the nine-to-eleven-month regimen for DR-TB. Promote research on universal TB regimens and drug susceptibility testing (DST) for resistance monitoring. Ensure equitable and rapid access to DST for fluoroquinolones to reduce diagnostic delays. 4. Implementation: Provide cost-effectiveness data on new regimens. Enhance training for healthcare workers in DR-TB management. Support person-centered care approaches, including social, psychological, and economic support. Conclusion The consultation emphasized the importance of evidence-based policy updates, equitable access to diagnostics and treatment, and the need for ongoing research to address gaps in TB prevention, diagnosis, and care. The outcomes of this meeting aim to guide global efforts in achieving the targets of the WHO End TB Strategy.
